content_html:
The Panic of 1873 was a financial crisis that triggered an economic depression in Europe and North America that lasted from 1873 to 1877, continuing until 1879 in the French Third Republic and in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. In Britain, the panic started two decades of economic stagnation known as the "Long Depression" that weakened the country's economic leadership.[1] In the United States, the period of economic stagnation was known as the "Great Depression" until the events of 1929 and the early 1930s set a new standard.[2]

The Panic of 1873 and the subsequent depression had several underlying causes, of which economic historians debate the relative importance. American inflation, rampant speculative investments (overwhelmingly in railroads), the demonetization of silver in Germany and the United States, ripples from economic dislocation in Europe resulting from the Franco-Prussian War (1870–1871), and major property losses in the Great Chicago Fire (1871) and the Great Boston Fire (1872) all contributed to a massive strain on bank reserves, which in New York City plummeted from $50 million to $17 million between September and October 1873. The first symptoms of the crisis were financial failures in Vienna, the capital of Austria-Hungary, which spread to most of Europe and to North America by 1873.

Europe and North America experienced an economic boom built on bond investments, and world trade expanded. After 1850 two banking institutions issued 70% of global bonds, the Rothschild family and the Barings Bank.[3]

Germany and Austria-Hungary

[edit]

Economic expansion took place in Germany and Austria-Hungary, where the period from German unification in 1870 and 1871 to the crash in 1873 came to be called the Gründerjahre ("Founders' Years"). A liberalized incorporation law in Germany gave impetus to a rise in IPOs the foundation of enterprises such as Deutsche Bank, and the incorporation of established ones. After the Franco-Prussian War in 1871 there was a massive influx of capital from the payment by France of war reparations. According to Liaquat Ahamed "German states paid off their debts. So they retired all their government bonds, and the savers who held German government bonds were left with cash. The question was what to do with this cash." It was invested in the stock market and fueled speculation in railways, factories, docks, and steamships, the same industrial branches that expanded unsustainably in the United States.[4] In the immediate aftermath of his victory against France, Otto von Bismarck also began the process of silver demonetization and placed Germany on the gold standard.[5] The process began on 23 November 1871 and culminated in the introduction of the gold mark on 9 July 1873 as the currency for the newly founded German Empire, replacing the silver coins of all constituent lands. Demonetization of silver was thus a common element in the crises on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean.

On 9 May 1873, the Vienna Stock Exchange crashed because it was unable to sustain the bubble of false expansion, insolvencies, and dishonest manipulations.[citation needed] A series of Viennese bank failures ensued, causing a contraction of the money available for business lending. One of the more famous people who went bankrupt in 1873 was Stephan Keglevich of Vienna, a relative of Gábor Keglevich who had been the master of the royal treasury (1842–1848) and in 1845 had co-founded a financial association to fund the expansion of Hungarian industry and to protect the loan repayments, similar to the 1870 Kreditschutzverband, an Austrian association for the protection of creditors and the interests of its members in cases of bankruptcy. That made it possible for several Austrian banks to be established in 1873 after the Vienna Stock Exchange crash.[6]

In Berlin, the railway empire of Bethel Henry Strousberg crashed after a ruinous settlement with the government of Romania, bursting the speculation bubble in Germany. The contraction of the German economy was exacerbated by the conclusion of payments by France in September 1873. Two years after the foundation of the German Empire, the panic came and became known as the Gründerkrach or "Founders' Crash".[7][8][9] In 1865, Keglevich and Strousberg had come into direct competition in a project in what is now Slovakia. In 1870 the Hungarian government, and in 1872 the Emperor-King Franz Joseph of Austria, resolved the question of the competing projects.[10][11]

Although the collapse of the foreign loan financing had been predicted, the events of that year were in themselves comparatively unimportant. Buda, the old capital of Hungary, and Óbuda were officially united with Pest,[12] thus creating Budapest in 1873. The difference in stability between Vienna and Berlin had the effect that the French indemnity to Germany flowed into Austria and Russia, but the indemnity payments aggravated the crisis in Austria, which had benefited by the accumulation of capital not only in Germany but also in England, the Netherlands, Belgium, France, and Russia.[13]

Recovery from the crash occurred much more quickly in Europe than in the United States.[14][15] Moreover, German businesses managed to avoid the sort of deep wage cuts that embittered American labor relations.[15] There was an anti-Semitic component to the economic recovery in Germany and Austria, as small investors blamed Jews for their losses in the crash.[16][17] The Neuer Sozial-Demokrat newspaper of the General German Workers' Association (ADAV) published several articles blaming Gerson von Bleichröder for the stock market crash. An October 29 article called Bleichröder "Bismarck's Jew".[18]

Soon, more luxury hotels and villas were built in Opatija, and a railway line was extended in 1873 from the Vienna–Trieste line to Rijeka (Fiume), making it possible to go by tram from there to Opatija. The strong increase of port traffic generated a permanent demand for expansion.[19] The Suez Canal was opened in 1869.[20] 1875–1890 became "the golden years" of Giovanni de Ciotta in Rijeka.

The crash is central in the 1877 novel The Breaking of the Storm by the German writer Friedrich Spielhagen. A portrayal of German business life in the 1870s, the literary scholar Jeffrey L. Sammons has described it as "the major fictional treatment of the financial crash of the 1870s as a harbinger of the predatory but erratic capitalism that was to become characteristic of the Reich".[21]

The opening of the Suez Canal was one of the causes of the Panic of 1873 because goods from the Far East had previously been carried in sailing vessels around the Cape of Good Hope and had been stored in British warehouses. As sailing vessels were not adaptable for use through the Suez Canal (because the prevailing winds of the Mediterranean Sea blow from west to east), the British entrepôt trade suffered.[22]

When the crisis came, the Bank of England raised interest rates to 9 percent. Despite this, Britain did not experience the scale of financial mayhem seen in America and Central Europe, perhaps forestalled by an expectation that the liquidity-constraining provisions of the Bank Charter Act 1844 would be suspended as they had been in the crises of 1847, 1857, and 1866. The ensuing economic downturn in Britain seems to have been muted – "stagnant" but without a "decline in aggregate output".[23] However, there was heavy unemployment in the basic industries of coal, iron and steel, engineering, and shipbuilding, especially in 1873, 1886, and 1893.[1]

Comparison with Germany

[edit]

From 1873 to 1896, a period sometimes referred to as the Long Depression, most European countries experienced a drastic fall in prices. Still, many corporations were able to reduce production costs and achieve better productivity rates with industrial production increasing by 40% in Britain and by over 100% in Germany.[citation needed] A comparison of capital formation rates in both countries helps to account for the different industrial growth rates. During the depression, the British ratio of net national capital formation to net national product fell from 11.5% to 6.0%, but the German ratio rose from 10.6% to 15.9%.[citation needed] Britain took the course of static supply adjustment, but Germany stimulated effective demand and expanded industrial supply capacity by increasing and adjusting capital formation. For example, Germany dramatically increased investment of social overhead capital, such as in the management of electric power transmission lines, roads, and railroads, thereby stimulating industrial demand in that country, but similar investment stagnated or decreased in Britain. The resulting difference in capital formation accounts for the divergent levels of industrial production in the two countries and the different growth rates during and after the depression.[24]

The discovery of large quantities of silver in the United States and several European colonies caused the panic of 1873 and thus a decline in the value of silver relative to gold, devaluing India's standard currency.

In the Cape Colony, the panic caused bankruptcies, rising unemployment, a pause in public works, and a major trade slump that lasted until the discovery of gold in 1886.[25]

In the Ottoman Empire rates of growth of foreign trade dropped, external terms of trade deteriorated, declining wheat prices affected peasant producers, and the establishment of European control over Ottoman finances led to large debt payments abroad. The growth rates of agricultural and aggregate production were also lower during the Long Depression than the later period.[26]

Latin Monetary Union

[edit]

The general demonetization and cheapening of silver caused the Latin Monetary Union in 1873 to suspend the conversion of silver to coins.[27][28]

The American Civil War (1861–1865) was followed by a boom in railroad construction. 33,000 miles (53,000 km) of track were laid across the country between 1868 and 1873,[29] with much of the craze in railroad investment being driven by government land grants and subsidies to the railroads.[30] The railroad industry was the largest employer outside of agriculture and involved large amounts of money and risk. A large infusion of cash from speculators caused spectacular growth in the industry and in the construction of docks, factories, and ancillary facilities. Most capital was involved in projects offering no immediate or early returns.[31]

Coinage Act of 1873

[edit]

A period of economic overexpansion arose from the northern railroad boom before a series of economic setbacks: the Black Friday panic of 1869, the Chicago fire of 1871, an outbreak of equine influenza and the Boston fire of 1872.

The decision of the German Empire to cease minting silver thaler coins in 1871 caused a drop in demand and downward pressure on the value of silver, which in turn affected the U.S. since much of the supply of silver was mined there. As a result, the U.S. Congress passed the Coinage Act of 1873, which changed the national silver policy. Before the act, the U.S. had backed its currency with both gold and silver and minted both types of coins. The act moved the U.S. to a de facto gold standard, which meant it would no longer buy silver at a statutory price or convert silver from the public into silver coins, but it would still mint silver dollars for export in the form of trade dollars.[32]

The act had the immediate effect of depressing silver prices, hurting Western mining interests who labeled the act "The Crime of '73", but its effect was offset somewhat by the introduction of a silver trade dollar for use in Asia and the discovery of silver deposits at Virginia City, Nevada, that resulted in new investment in mining activity.[33] The act also reduced the domestic money supply, raising interest rates and hurting farmers and others who normally carried heavy debt loads. The resulting outcry raised serious questions about how long the new policy would last.[34] The perception of U.S. instability in its monetary policy caused investors to shy away from long-term obligations, particularly long-term bonds. The problem was compounded by the railroad boom, which was then in its later stages.

Jay Cooke & Company fails

[edit]

In September 1873, Jay Cooke & Company, a major component of the country's banking establishment, found itself unable to market several million dollars in Northern Pacific Railway bonds. Jay Cooke's firm, like many others, had invested heavily in the railroads. Some investment banks were then anxious for more capital for their enterprises. U.S. President Ulysses S. Grant's monetary policy of contracting the money supply and thus raising interest rates made matters worse for those in debt. Businesses were expanding, but the money they needed to finance that growth was becoming scarcer.

Cooke and other entrepreneurs had planned to build the second transcontinental railroad, the Northern Pacific Railway. Cooke's firm provided the financing, and ground for the line was broken near Duluth, Minnesota, on 15 February 1870. The railroad had borrowed more than $1.5 million from Jay Cooke & Company but was incapable of paying it back.[35] An expanding funding gap became harder to resolve due to the Credit Mobilier scandal.[36] Due to the financial crises in Europe, Cooke could not sell the securities abroad.[35] Just as Cooke was about to access a $300 million government loan in September 1873, reports circulated that his firm's credit had become nearly worthless. On 18 September, the firm declared bankruptcy.[35][37]

Many U.S. insurance companies went out of business, as the deteriorating financial conditions created solvency problems for life insurers. The common factor of the surviving companies was that all marketed tontines.[38]

The failure of Cooke's bank and soon afterward of Henry Clews' set off a chain reaction of bank failures and temporarily closed the New York Stock Exchange. Factories began to lay off workers as the country slipped into depression. The effects of the panic were quickly felt in New York (where 25% of workers became unemployed) and more slowly in Chicago, Virginia City, Nevada (where silver mining was active), and San Francisco.[36][39][40]

The New York Stock Exchange closed for ten days starting on 20 September.[41] By November, 55 of the nation's railroads had failed, and another 60 had gone bankrupt by the first anniversary of the crisis.[42] Construction of rail lines, formerly one of the backbones of the economy, plummeted from 7,500 miles (12,100 km) of track in 1872 to just 1,600 miles (2,600 km) in 1875,[42] and 18,000 businesses failed between 1873 and 1875. Unemployment peaked in 1878 at 8.25%.[43] Building construction was halted, wages were cut, real estate values fell, and corporate profits vanished.[44]

In 1874, Congress passed "the Ferry Bill"[45] to allow for the printing of currency, increasing inflation and reducing the value of debts.[46] The bill was vetoed by President Grant.[46] The following year, Congress passed the Specie Resumption Act of 1875, which would back United States currency with gold.[46] Backing American currency with gold helped curb inflation and stabilize the dollar.[46]

The railroad industry had seen major growth in the decades before 1873, driven in part by strong European interest in bonds issued by railroad companies.[47][48] The failure of Jay Cooke & Co., heavily invested in railroad bonds, triggered a crisis in the railroad industry.

In 1877, steep wage cuts led railroad workers to launch the series of protests and riots later dubbed the Great Railroad Strike. Initial protests broke out in Martinsburg, West Virginia, after the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad (B&O) cut workers' pay for the third time in a year. West Virginia Governor Henry M. Mathews sent the militia, under Colonel Charles J. Faulkner, to restore order but was unsuccessful, largely because the militia sympathized with the workers. Mathews called on President Rutherford B. Hayes for federal assistance, and Hayes dispatched federal troops. That restored peace to Martinsburg but proved controversial, with many newspapers[specify] critical of Mathews' characterization of the strikes as an "insurrection", rather than an act of desperation and frustration. The Martinsburg Statesman recorded a striking worker's perspective that he "might as well die by the bullet as to starve to death by inches".[49]

Within a week, similar protests had erupted in other cities.[50][51] In Baltimore, strikers set fire to buildings owned by B&O and an outnumbered militia guard division opened fire when they were surrounded by rioters, killing 10 and injuring 25 more,[52] leading to a days-long standoff at Camden Yards. In New York, striking workers began throwing objects at arriving trains, prompting a response from local police.[53] Pennsylvania saw perhaps the worst violence of the railroad strikes;[54][55] notably in the Pittsburgh railroad strike of 1877, the Reading Railroad massacre and the Scranton general strike. In Chicago, striking workers brought freight and passenger trains to a standstill, leading to an order from Judge Thomas Drummond that such actions were illegal.[56] The United States Marshals Service responded by arresting dozens of strikers. In Missouri, strikers also brought rail traffic to a halt, and at least 18 people died in conflicts.[57]

In July 1877, the market for lumber crashed, leading several Michigan lumber companies to go bankrupt.[58] Within a year, the effects of this second business slump reached all the way to California.[59]

The depression ended in the spring of 1879, but tension between workers and the leaders of banking and manufacturing interests lingered on.[60] Poor economic conditions caused voters to turn against the Republican Party. In the 1874 congressional elections, the Democratic Party assumed control of the House for the first time since the Civil War.[61]

Public opinion made it difficult for the Grant administration to develop a coherent policy on the Southern states, and the North began to steer away from Reconstruction. Ambitious railroad building programs crashed across the South, leaving most states deep in debt and burdened with heavy taxes. Retrenchment was a common response of the South to state debts during the depression. One by one, each state fell to the Democrats in the South, and the Republicans lost power.

The end of the crisis coincided with the beginning of the great wave of immigration to the United States, which lasted until the early 1920s.[62][63]

Global protectionism

[edit]

After the 1873 depression, agricultural and industrial groups lobbied for protective tariffs. Conservative politicians such as Bismarck shifted from classical liberal economic policies in the 1870s, embracing many economic interventionist policies, including high tariffs, nationalization of railroads, and compulsory social insurance.[64][65][66] The political and economic nationalism also reduced the fortunes of the German and Canadian classical liberal parties. France, like Britain, entered into a prolonged stagnation that extended to 1897. The French attempted to deal with their economic problems by the implementation of tariffs. French laws implemented in 1880 and 1892 imposed stiff tariffs on many agricultural and industrial imports.[67] The U.S. continued to be protectionist.[68][69]

content_text: A bank run on the Fourth National Bank No. 20 Nassau Street, New York City, from Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper, 4 October 1873 The Panic of 1873 was a financial crisis that triggered an economic depression in Europe and North America that lasted from 1873 to 1877, continuing until 1879 in the French Third Republic and in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. In Britain, the panic started two decades of economic stagnation known as the "Long Depression" that weakened the country's economic leadership.[1] In the United States, the period of economic stagnation was known as the "Great Depression" until the events of 1929 and the early 1930s set a new standard.[2] The Panic of 1873 and the subsequent depression had several underlying causes, of which economic historians debate the relative importance. American inflation, rampant speculative investments (overwhelmingly in railroads), the demonetization of silver in Germany and the United States, ripples from economic dislocation in Europe resulting from the Franco-Prussian War (1870–1871), and major property losses in the Great Chicago Fire (1871) and the Great Boston Fire (1872) all contributed to a massive strain on bank reserves, which in New York City plummeted from $50 million to $17 million between September and October 1873. The first symptoms of the crisis were financial failures in Vienna, the capital of Austria-Hungary, which spread to most of Europe and to North America by 1873. Europe and North America experienced an economic boom built on bond investments, and world trade expanded. After 1850 two banking institutions issued 70% of global bonds, the Rothschild family and the Barings Bank.[3] Germany and Austria-Hungary[edit] Black Friday, 9 May 1873, Vienna Stocks Economic expansion took place in Germany and Austria-Hungary, where the period from German unification in 1870 and 1871 to the crash in 1873 came to be called the Gründerjahre ("Founders' Years"). A liberalized incorporation law in Germany gave impetus to a rise in IPOs the foundation of enterprises such as Deutsche Bank, and the incorporation of established ones. After the Franco-Prussian War in 1871 there was a massive influx of capital from the payment by France of war reparations. According to Liaquat Ahamed "German states paid off their debts. So they retired all their government bonds, and the savers who held German government bonds were left with cash. The question was what to do with this cash." It was invested in the stock market and fueled speculation in railways, factories, docks, and steamships, the same industrial branches that expanded unsustainably in the United States.[4] In the immediate aftermath of his victory against France, Otto von Bismarck also began the process of silver demonetization and placed Germany on the gold standard.[5] The process began on 23 November 1871 and culminated in the introduction of the gold mark on 9 July 1873 as the currency for the newly founded German Empire, replacing the silver coins of all constituent lands. Demonetization of silver was thus a common element in the crises on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean. On 9 May 1873, the Vienna Stock Exchange crashed because it was unable to sustain the bubble of false expansion, insolvencies, and dishonest manipulations.[citation needed] A series of Viennese bank failures ensued, causing a contraction of the money available for business lending. One of the more famous people who went bankrupt in 1873 was Stephan Keglevich of Vienna, a relative of Gábor Keglevich who had been the master of the royal treasury (1842–1848) and in 1845 had co-founded a financial association to fund the expansion of Hungarian industry and to protect the loan repayments, similar to the 1870 Kreditschutzverband, an Austrian association for the protection of creditors and the interests of its members in cases of bankruptcy. That made it possible for several Austrian banks to be established in 1873 after the Vienna Stock Exchange crash.[6] In Berlin, the railway empire of Bethel Henry Strousberg crashed after a ruinous settlement with the government of Romania, bursting the speculation bubble in Germany. The contraction of the German economy was exacerbated by the conclusion of payments by France in September 1873. Two years after the foundation of the German Empire, the panic came and became known as the Gründerkrach or "Founders' Crash".[7][8][9] In 1865, Keglevich and Strousberg had come into direct competition in a project in what is now Slovakia. In 1870 the Hungarian government, and in 1872 the Emperor-King Franz Joseph of Austria, resolved the question of the competing projects.[10][11] Although the collapse of the foreign loan financing had been predicted, the events of that year were in themselves comparatively unimportant. Buda, the old capital of Hungary, and Óbuda were officially united with Pest,[12] thus creating Budapest in 1873. The difference in stability between Vienna and Berlin had the effect that the French indemnity to Germany flowed into Austria and Russia, but the indemnity payments aggravated the crisis in Austria, which had benefited by the accumulation of capital not only in Germany but also in England, the Netherlands, Belgium, France, and Russia.[13] Recovery from the crash occurred much more quickly in Europe than in the United States.[14][15] Moreover, German businesses managed to avoid the sort of deep wage cuts that embittered American labor relations.[15] There was an anti-Semitic component to the economic recovery in Germany and Austria, as small investors blamed Jews for their losses in the crash.[16][17] The Neuer Sozial-Demokrat newspaper of the General German Workers' Association (ADAV) published several articles blaming Gerson von Bleichröder for the stock market crash. An October 29 article called Bleichröder "Bismarck's Jew".[18] Soon, more luxury hotels and villas were built in Opatija, and a railway line was extended in 1873 from the Vienna–Trieste line to Rijeka (Fiume), making it possible to go by tram from there to Opatija. The strong increase of port traffic generated a permanent demand for expansion.[19] The Suez Canal was opened in 1869.[20] 1875–1890 became "the golden years" of Giovanni de Ciotta in Rijeka. The crash is central in the 1877 novel The Breaking of the Storm by the German writer Friedrich Spielhagen. A portrayal of German business life in the 1870s, the literary scholar Jeffrey L. Sammons has described it as "the major fictional treatment of the financial crash of the 1870s as a harbinger of the predatory but erratic capitalism that was to become characteristic of the Reich".[21] The opening of the Suez Canal was one of the causes of the Panic of 1873 because goods from the Far East had previously been carried in sailing vessels around the Cape of Good Hope and had been stored in British warehouses. As sailing vessels were not adaptable for use through the Suez Canal (because the prevailing winds of the Mediterranean Sea blow from west to east), the British entrepôt trade suffered.[22] When the crisis came, the Bank of England raised interest rates to 9 percent. Despite this, Britain did not experience the scale of financial mayhem seen in America and Central Europe, perhaps forestalled by an expectation that the liquidity-constraining provisions of the Bank Charter Act 1844 would be suspended as they had been in the crises of 1847, 1857, and 1866. The ensuing economic downturn in Britain seems to have been muted – "stagnant" but without a "decline in aggregate output".[23] However, there was heavy unemployment in the basic industries of coal, iron and steel, engineering, and shipbuilding, especially in 1873, 1886, and 1893.[1] Comparison with Germany[edit] From 1873 to 1896, a period sometimes referred to as the Long Depression, most European countries experienced a drastic fall in prices. Still, many corporations were able to reduce production costs and achieve better productivity rates with industrial production increasing by 40% in Britain and by over 100% in Germany.[citation needed] A comparison of capital formation rates in both countries helps to account for the different industrial growth rates. During the depression, the British ratio of net national capital formation to net national product fell from 11.5% to 6.0%, but the German ratio rose from 10.6% to 15.9%.[citation needed] Britain took the course of static supply adjustment, but Germany stimulated effective demand and expanded industrial supply capacity by increasing and adjusting capital formation. For example, Germany dramatically increased investment of social overhead capital, such as in the management of electric power transmission lines, roads, and railroads, thereby stimulating industrial demand in that country, but similar investment stagnated or decreased in Britain. The resulting difference in capital formation accounts for the divergent levels of industrial production in the two countries and the different growth rates during and after the depression.[24] The discovery of large quantities of silver in the United States and several European colonies caused the panic of 1873 and thus a decline in the value of silver relative to gold, devaluing India's standard currency. In the Cape Colony, the panic caused bankruptcies, rising unemployment, a pause in public works, and a major trade slump that lasted until the discovery of gold in 1886.[25] In the Ottoman Empire rates of growth of foreign trade dropped, external terms of trade deteriorated, declining wheat prices affected peasant producers, and the establishment of European control over Ottoman finances led to large debt payments abroad. The growth rates of agricultural and aggregate production were also lower during the Long Depression than the later period.[26] Latin Monetary Union[edit] The general demonetization and cheapening of silver caused the Latin Monetary Union in 1873 to suspend the conversion of silver to coins.[27][28] The American Civil War (1861–1865) was followed by a boom in railroad construction. 33,000 miles (53,000 km) of track were laid across the country between 1868 and 1873,[29] with much of the craze in railroad investment being driven by government land grants and subsidies to the railroads.[30] The railroad industry was the largest employer outside of agriculture and involved large amounts of money and risk. A large infusion of cash from speculators caused spectacular growth in the industry and in the construction of docks, factories, and ancillary facilities. Most capital was involved in projects offering no immediate or early returns.[31] Coinage Act of 1873[edit] A period of economic overexpansion arose from the northern railroad boom before a series of economic setbacks: the Black Friday panic of 1869, the Chicago fire of 1871, an outbreak of equine influenza and the Boston fire of 1872. The decision of the German Empire to cease minting silver thaler coins in 1871 caused a drop in demand and downward pressure on the value of silver, which in turn affected the U.S. since much of the supply of silver was mined there. As a result, the U.S. Congress passed the Coinage Act of 1873, which changed the national silver policy. Before the act, the U.S. had backed its currency with both gold and silver and minted both types of coins. The act moved the U.S. to a de facto gold standard, which meant it would no longer buy silver at a statutory price or convert silver from the public into silver coins, but it would still mint silver dollars for export in the form of trade dollars.[32] The act had the immediate effect of depressing silver prices, hurting Western mining interests who labeled the act "The Crime of '73", but its effect was offset somewhat by the introduction of a silver trade dollar for use in Asia and the discovery of silver deposits at Virginia City, Nevada, that resulted in new investment in mining activity.[33] The act also reduced the domestic money supply, raising interest rates and hurting farmers and others who normally carried heavy debt loads. The resulting outcry raised serious questions about how long the new policy would last.[34] The perception of U.S. instability in its monetary policy caused investors to shy away from long-term obligations, particularly long-term bonds. The problem was compounded by the railroad boom, which was then in its later stages. Jay Cooke & Company fails[edit] In September 1873, Jay Cooke & Company, a major component of the country's banking establishment, found itself unable to market several million dollars in Northern Pacific Railway bonds. Jay Cooke's firm, like many others, had invested heavily in the railroads. Some investment banks were then anxious for more capital for their enterprises. U.S. President Ulysses S. Grant's monetary policy of contracting the money supply and thus raising interest rates made matters worse for those in debt. Businesses were expanding, but the money they needed to finance that growth was becoming scarcer. Cooke and other entrepreneurs had planned to build the second transcontinental railroad, the Northern Pacific Railway. Cooke's firm provided the financing, and ground for the line was broken near Duluth, Minnesota, on 15 February 1870. The railroad had borrowed more than $1.5 million from Jay Cooke & Company but was incapable of paying it back.[35] An expanding funding gap became harder to resolve due to the Credit Mobilier scandal.[36] Due to the financial crises in Europe, Cooke could not sell the securities abroad.[35] Just as Cooke was about to access a $300 million government loan in September 1873, reports circulated that his firm's credit had become nearly worthless. On 18 September, the firm declared bankruptcy.[35][37] Many U.S. insurance companies went out of business, as the deteriorating financial conditions created solvency problems for life insurers. The common factor of the surviving companies was that all marketed tontines.[38] New York police violently attacking unemployed workers in Tompkins Square Park, 1874 The failure of Cooke's bank and soon afterward of Henry Clews' set off a chain reaction of bank failures and temporarily closed the New York Stock Exchange. Factories began to lay off workers as the country slipped into depression. The effects of the panic were quickly felt in New York (where 25% of workers became unemployed) and more slowly in Chicago, Virginia City, Nevada (where silver mining was active), and San Francisco.[36][39][40] The New York Stock Exchange closed for ten days starting on 20 September.[41] By November, 55 of the nation's railroads had failed, and another 60 had gone bankrupt by the first anniversary of the crisis.[42] Construction of rail lines, formerly one of the backbones of the economy, plummeted from 7,500 miles (12,100 km) of track in 1872 to just 1,600 miles (2,600 km) in 1875,[42] and 18,000 businesses failed between 1873 and 1875. Unemployment peaked in 1878 at 8.25%.[43] Building construction was halted, wages were cut, real estate values fell, and corporate profits vanished.[44] In 1874, Congress passed "the Ferry Bill"[45] to allow for the printing of currency, increasing inflation and reducing the value of debts.[46] The bill was vetoed by President Grant.[46] The following year, Congress passed the Specie Resumption Act of 1875, which would back United States currency with gold.[46] Backing American currency with gold helped curb inflation and stabilize the dollar.[46] The railroad industry had seen major growth in the decades before 1873, driven in part by strong European interest in bonds issued by railroad companies.[47][48] The failure of Jay Cooke & Co., heavily invested in railroad bonds, triggered a crisis in the railroad industry. In 1877, steep wage cuts led railroad workers to launch the series of protests and riots later dubbed the Great Railroad Strike. Initial protests broke out in Martinsburg, West Virginia, after the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad (B&O) cut workers' pay for the third time in a year. West Virginia Governor Henry M. Mathews sent the militia, under Colonel Charles J. Faulkner, to restore order but was unsuccessful, largely because the militia sympathized with the workers. Mathews called on President Rutherford B. Hayes for federal assistance, and Hayes dispatched federal troops. That restored peace to Martinsburg but proved controversial, with many newspapers[specify] critical of Mathews' characterization of the strikes as an "insurrection", rather than an act of desperation and frustration. The Martinsburg Statesman recorded a striking worker's perspective that he "might as well die by the bullet as to starve to death by inches".[49] Within a week, similar protests had erupted in other cities.[50][51] In Baltimore, strikers set fire to buildings owned by B&O and an outnumbered militia guard division opened fire when they were surrounded by rioters, killing 10 and injuring 25 more,[52] leading to a days-long standoff at Camden Yards. In New York, striking workers began throwing objects at arriving trains, prompting a response from local police.[53] Pennsylvania saw perhaps the worst violence of the railroad strikes;[54][55] notably in the Pittsburgh railroad strike of 1877, the Reading Railroad massacre and the Scranton general strike. In Chicago, striking workers brought freight and passenger trains to a standstill, leading to an order from Judge Thomas Drummond that such actions were illegal.[56] The United States Marshals Service responded by arresting dozens of strikers. In Missouri, strikers also brought rail traffic to a halt, and at least 18 people died in conflicts.[57] In July 1877, the market for lumber crashed, leading several Michigan lumber companies to go bankrupt.[58] Within a year, the effects of this second business slump reached all the way to California.[59] The depression ended in the spring of 1879, but tension between workers and the leaders of banking and manufacturing interests lingered on.[60] Poor economic conditions caused voters to turn against the Republican Party. In the 1874 congressional elections, the Democratic Party assumed control of the House for the first time since the Civil War.[61] Public opinion made it difficult for the Grant administration to develop a coherent policy on the Southern states, and the North began to steer away from Reconstruction. Ambitious railroad building programs crashed across the South, leaving most states deep in debt and burdened with heavy taxes. Retrenchment was a common response of the South to state debts during the depression. One by one, each state fell to the Democrats in the South, and the Republicans lost power. The end of the crisis coincided with the beginning of the great wave of immigration to the United States, which lasted until the early 1920s.[62][63] Global protectionism[edit] After the 1873 depression, agricultural and industrial groups lobbied for protective tariffs. Conservative politicians such as Bismarck shifted from classical liberal economic policies in the 1870s, embracing many economic interventionist policies, including high tariffs, nationalization of railroads, and compulsory social insurance.[64][65][66] The political and economic nationalism also reduced the fortunes of the German and Canadian classical liberal parties. France, like Britain, entered into a prolonged stagnation that extended to 1897. The French attempted to deal with their economic problems by the implementation of tariffs. The first symptoms of the crisis were financial failures in Vienna, the capital of Austria-Hungary, which spread to most of Europe and to North America by 1873.

blocks.html_en: Comparison with Germany
[edit]

From 1873 to 1896, a period sometimes referred to as the Long Depression, most European countries experienced a drastic fall in prices. Still, many corporations were able to reduce production costs and achieve better productivity rates with industrial production increasing by 40% in Britain and by over 100% in Germany.[citation needed] A comparison of capital formation rates in both countries helps to account for the different industrial growth rates. During the depression, the British ratio of net national capital formation to net national product fell from 11.5% to 6.0%, but the German ratio rose from 10.6% to 15.9%.[citation needed] Britain took the course of static supply adjustment, but Germany stimulated effective demand and expanded industrial supply capacity by increasing and adjusting capital formation. For example, Germany dramatically increased investment of social overhead capital, such as in the management of electric power transmission lines, roads, and railroads, thereby stimulating industrial demand in that country, but similar investment stagnated or decreased in Britain. The resulting difference in capital formation accounts for the divergent levels of industrial production in the two countries and the different growth rates during and after the depression.[24]

sentences.en: Still, many corporations were able to reduce production costs and achieve better productivity rates with industrial production increasing by 40% in Britain and by over 100% in Germany.[citation needed] A comparison of capital formation rates in both countries helps to account for the different industrial growth rates.
sentences.zh: 尽管如此，许多企业还是能够降低生产成本并实现更高的生产率，英国的工业生产增长了 40%，德国的工业生产增长了 100% 以上。 [需要引用] 两国资本形成率的比较有助于解释不同的工业增长率。

sentences.en: During the depression, the British ratio of net national capital formation to net national product fell from 11.5% to 6.0%, but the German ratio rose from 10.6% to 15.9%.[citation needed] Britain took the course of static supply adjustment, but Germany stimulated effective demand and expanded industrial supply capacity by increasing and adjusting capital formation.
sentences.zh: 萧条时期，英国国民资本净形成与国民生产净值的比率从11.5%下降到6.0%，而德国则从10.6%上升到15.9%。英国采取的是静态供给调整路线，而德国则通过增加和调整资本形成来刺激有效需求，扩大工业供给能力。

sentences.en: For example, Germany dramatically increased investment of social overhead capital, such as in the management of electric power transmission lines, roads, and railroads, thereby stimulating industrial demand in that country, but similar investment stagnated or decreased in Britain.
sentences.zh: 例如，德国大幅增加了社会间接资本投资，例如输电线路、公路和铁路的管理，从而刺激了该国的工业需求，但英国的类似投资却停滞或减少。

sentences.en: The resulting difference in capital formation accounts for the divergent levels of industrial production in the two countries and the different growth rates during and after the depression.[24]
sentences.zh: 由此产生的资本形成差异导致了两国工业生产水平的不同以及萧条期间和之后增长率的不同。 [24]

blocks.html_en: Coinage Act of 1873
[edit]

A period of economic overexpansion arose from the northern railroad boom before a series of economic setbacks: the Black Friday panic of 1869, the Chicago fire of 1871, an outbreak of equine influenza and the Boston fire of 1872.

sentences.en: A period of economic overexpansion arose from the northern railroad boom before a series of economic setbacks: the Black Friday panic of 1869, the Chicago fire of 1871, an outbreak of equine influenza and the Boston fire of 1872.
sentences.zh: 北部铁路繁荣引发了一段经济过度扩张时期，随后出现了一系列经济挫折：1869 年的黑色星期五恐慌、1871 年的芝加哥火灾、马流感的爆发和 1872 年的波士顿火灾。

blocks.html_en: The decision of the German Empire to cease minting silver thaler coins in 1871 caused a drop in demand and downward pressure on the value of silver, which in turn affected the U.S. since much of the supply of silver was mined there. As a result, the U.S. Congress passed the Coinage Act of 1873, which changed the national silver policy. Before the act, the U.S. had backed its currency with both gold and silver and minted both types of coins. The act moved the U.S. to a de facto gold standard, which meant it would no longer buy silver at a statutory price or convert silver from the public into silver coins, but it would still mint silver dollars for export in the form of trade dollars.[32]

sentences.en: The decision of the German Empire to cease minting silver thaler coins in 1871 caused a drop in demand and downward pressure on the value of silver, which in turn affected the U.S. since much of the supply of silver was mined there.

sentences.en: As a result, the U.S. Congress passed the Coinage Act of 1873, which changed the national silver policy.
sentences.zh: 结果，美国国会通过了1873年的《铸币法案》，改变了国家白银政策。

sentences.en: Before the act, the U.S. had backed its currency with both gold and silver and minted both types of coins.
sentences.zh: 在该法案出台之前，美国用黄金和白银来支持其货币，并铸造了这两种类型的硬币。

sentences.en: The act moved the U.S. to a de facto gold standard, which meant it would no longer buy silver at a statutory price or convert silver from the public into silver coins, but it would still mint silver dollars for export in the form of trade dollars.[32]
sentences.zh: 该法案使美国转向事实上的金本位，这意味着美国将不再以法定价格购买白银或将公众的白银转换成银币，但仍会铸造银元以贸易美元的形式出口。 [32]

blocks.html_en: The act had the immediate effect of depressing silver prices, hurting Western mining interests who labeled the act "The Crime of '73", but its effect was offset somewhat by the introduction of a silver trade dollar for use in Asia and the discovery of silver deposits at Virginia City, Nevada, that resulted in new investment in mining activity.[33] The act also reduced the domestic money supply, raising interest rates and hurting farmers and others who normally carried heavy debt loads. The resulting outcry raised serious questions about how long the new policy would last.[34] The perception of U.S. instability in its monetary policy caused investors to shy away from long-term obligations, particularly long-term bonds. The problem was compounded by the railroad boom, which was then in its later stages.

blocks.html_en: Jay Cooke & Company fails
[edit]

In September 1873, Jay Cooke & Company, a major component of the country's banking establishment, found itself unable to market several million dollars in Northern Pacific Railway bonds. Jay Cooke's firm, like many others, had invested heavily in the railroads. Some investment banks were then anxious for more capital for their enterprises. U.S. President Ulysses S. Grant's monetary policy of contracting the money supply and thus raising interest rates made matters worse for those in debt. Businesses were expanding, but the money they needed to finance that growth was becoming scarcer.

blocks.html_en: Cooke and other entrepreneurs had planned to build the second transcontinental railroad, the Northern Pacific Railway. Cooke's firm provided the financing, and ground for the line was broken near Duluth, Minnesota, on 15 February 1870. The railroad had borrowed more than $1.5 million from Jay Cooke & Company but was incapable of paying it back.[35] An expanding funding gap became harder to resolve due to the Credit Mobilier scandal.[36] Due to the financial crises in Europe, Cooke could not sell the securities abroad.[35] Just as Cooke was about to access a $300 million government loan in September 1873, reports circulated that his firm's credit had become nearly worthless. On 18 September, the firm declared bankruptcy.[35][37]

blocks.html_en: In 1877, steep wage cuts led railroad workers to launch the series of protests and riots later dubbed the Great Railroad Strike. Initial protests broke out in Martinsburg, West Virginia, after the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad (B&O) cut workers' pay for the third time in a year. West Virginia Governor Henry M. Mathews sent the militia, under Colonel Charles J. Faulkner, to restore order but was unsuccessful, largely because the militia sympathized with the workers. Mathews called on President Rutherford B. Hayes for federal assistance, and Hayes dispatched federal troops. That restored peace to Martinsburg but proved controversial, with many newspapers[specify] critical of Mathews' characterization of the strikes as an "insurrection", rather than an act of desperation and frustration. The Martinsburg Statesman recorded a striking worker's perspective that he "might as well die by the bullet as to starve to death by inches".[49]

blocks.html_en: Within a week, similar protests had erupted in other cities.[50][51] In Baltimore, strikers set fire to buildings owned by B&O and an outnumbered militia guard division opened fire when they were surrounded by rioters, killing 10 and injuring 25 more,[52] leading to a days-long standoff at Camden Yards. blocks.html_en: Global protectionism
[edit]

After the 1873 depression, agricultural and industrial groups lobbied for protective tariffs. Conservative politicians such as Bismarck shifted from classical liberal economic policies in the 1870s, embracing many economic interventionist policies, including high tariffs, nationalization of railroads, and compulsory social insurance.[64][65][66] The political and economic nationalism also reduced the fortunes of the German and Canadian classical liberal parties. France, like Britain, entered into a prolonged stagnation that extended to 1897. The French attempted to deal with their economic problems by the implementation of tariffs. French laws implemented in 1880 and 1892 imposed stiff tariffs on many agricultural and industrial imports.[67] The U.S. continued to be protectionist.[68][69]

content_html_zh:
1873年恐慌是一场金融危机，引发了欧洲和北美的经济萧条，从1873年持续到1877年，法兰西第三共和国和大不列颠及爱尔兰联合王国一直持续到1879年。 在英国，恐慌引发了长达二十年的经济停滞，被称为“长期萧条”，削弱了该国的经济领导地位。 [1]在美国，经济停滞时期被称为“大萧条”，直到 1929 年和 20 世纪 30 年代初的事件树立了新的标准。 [2]

1873 年的恐慌和随后的萧条有几个根本原因，经济历史学家对其中的相对重要性存在争议。 美国的通货膨胀、猖獗的投机投资（绝大多数是铁路）、德国和美国的白银废止、普法战争（1870-1871）造成的欧洲经济混乱的连锁反应，以及芝加哥大火（1871）和波士顿大火（1872）的重大财产损失，都导致银行准备金承受巨大压力，纽约市的准备金从 5000 万美元暴跌至 17 美元。 1873 年 9 月至 10 月期间，该数字为 100 万。 这场危机的最初症状是奥匈帝国首都维也纳的金融失败，到 1873 年危机蔓延到欧洲大部分地区和北美。

欧洲和北美经历了以债券投资为基础的经济繁荣，世界贸易不断扩大。 1850年后，罗斯柴尔德家族和巴林银行这两家银行机构发行了全球70%的债券。[3]

德国和奥匈帝国

[edit]

德国和奥匈帝国出现了经济扩张，从 1870 年和 1871 年德国统一到 1873 年崩溃的这段时期被称为 Gründerjahre（“创始人年”）。 德国自由化的公司法推动了德意志银行等企业的首次公开募股以及老牌企业的注册增加。 1871年普法战争后，法国支付战争赔款，资本大量涌入。 利亚卡特·艾哈迈德表示，“德国各州还清了债务。 因此，他们赎回了所有政府债券，而持有德国政府债券的储户则留下了现金。 问题是如何处理这笔现金。” 它投资于股票市场，并刺激了铁路、工厂、码头和轮船的投机，这些工业部门在美国不可持续地扩张。 [4]在战胜法国后，奥托·冯·俾斯麦也立即开始了白银非货币化进程，并将德国置于金本位制之下。 [5]这一过程始于 1871 年 11 月 23 日，最终于 1873 年 7 月 9 日引入金马克作为新成立的德意志帝国的货币，取代了所有领土的银币。 因此，白银非货币化是大西洋两岸危机的一个共同因素。

1873 年 5 月 9 日，维也纳证券交易所崩溃，因为它无法维持虚假扩张、破产和不诚实操纵的泡沫。[需要引用]一系列维也纳银行倒闭，导致可用于商业贷款的资金紧缩。 1873 年破产的最著名的人物之一是维也纳的史蒂芬·凯格列维奇 (Stephan Keglevich)，他是加博尔·凯格列维奇 (Gábor Keglevich) 的亲戚，加博尔·凯格列维奇 (Gábor Keglevich) 曾担任皇家财政部长 (1842-1848 年)，并于 1845 年与他人共同创立了一个金融协会，为匈牙利工业的扩张提供资金并保护贷款偿还，类似于 1870 年的 Kreditschutzverband（一个旨在保护匈牙利人财产的奥地利协会）。破产时债权人及其成员的利益。 这使得多家奥地利银行得以在 1873 年维也纳证券交易所崩溃后成立。 [6]

在柏林，伯特利·亨利·斯特劳斯伯格的铁路帝国在与罗马尼亚政府达成毁灭性和解后崩溃，打破了德国的投机泡沫。 1873 年 9 月法国结束付款，加剧了德国经济的萎缩。 德意志帝国建立两年后，恐慌来临，被称为 Gründerkrach 或“创始人崩溃”。[7][8][9] 1865 年，凯格列维奇和斯特劳斯伯格在现在斯洛伐克的一个项目上展开直接竞争。 1870 年，匈牙利政府和 1872 年奥地利皇帝弗朗茨·约瑟夫国王解决了竞争项目的问题。[10][11]

尽管外国贷款融资的崩溃已被预料到，但那一年发生的事件本身相对来说并不重要。 匈牙利旧都布达和奥布达正式与佩斯合并[12]，从而于 1873 年创建了布达佩斯。 维也纳和柏林之间的稳定性差异导致法国对德国的赔款流入奥地利和俄罗斯，但赔款支付却加剧了奥地利的危机，奥地利不仅受益于德国的资本积累，也受益于英国、荷兰、比利时、法国和俄罗斯的资本积累。 [13]

欧洲从崩溃中恢复的速度比美国快得多。[14][15]此外，德国企业设法避免了那种导致美国劳资关系恶化的大幅工资削减。 [15]德国和奥地利的经济复苏中存在反犹太成分，因为小投资者将经济危机中的损失归咎于犹太人。[16][17]德国工人总协会（ADAV）的《新社会民主党》报纸发表了多篇文章，指责格森·冯·布莱希罗德应为股市崩盘负责。 10 月 29 日的一篇文章称布莱希罗德为“俾斯麦的犹太人”。[18]

很快，更多的豪华酒店和别墅在奥帕蒂亚建成，铁路线于 1873 年从维也纳 - 的里雅斯特线延伸至里耶卡（阜姆），使得从那里乘坐电车前往奥帕蒂亚成为可能。 港口流量的强劲增长产生了永久性的扩建需求。[19]苏伊士运河于1869年开通。[20] 1875年至1890年成为乔瓦尼·德西奥塔在里耶卡的“黄金岁月”。

德国作家弗里德里希·斯皮尔哈根 (Friedrich Spielhagen) 于 1877 年出版的小说《风暴的爆发》中以这次事故为中心内容。 文学学者 Jeffrey L. 描绘了 1870 年代德国商业生活。 萨蒙斯将其描述为“对 1870 年代金融危机的主要虚构处理，将其视为掠夺性但不稳定的资本主义的预兆，而这种资本主义将成为帝国的特征”。 [21]

苏伊士运河的开通是1873年恐慌的原因之一，因为来自远东的货物此前都是通过帆船绕行好望角并储存在英国仓库中的。 由于帆船不适合通过苏伊士运河（因为地中海盛行风从西向东吹），英国转口贸易受到影响。 [22]

危机来临时，英国央行将利率提高至9%。 尽管如此，英国并没有经历美国和中欧那样规模的金融混乱，这或许是因为人们预期 1844 年《银行宪章法案》中的流动性限制条款将被暂停，就像它们在 1847 年、1857 年和 1866 年的危机中一样。 英国随之而来的经济衰退似乎已经减弱——“停滞”，但没有“总产出下降”。 [23]然而，煤炭、钢铁、工程、造船等基础工业却出现严重失业，特别是在1873年、1886年和1893年[1]。

与德国比较

[edit]

从 1873 年到 1896 年（有时被称为长期萧条），大多数欧洲国家经历了物价大幅下跌。 尽管如此，许多企业还是能够降低生产成本并实现更高的生产率，英国的工业生产增长了 40%，德国的工业生产增长了 100% 以上。 [需要引用] 两国资本形成率的比较有助于解释不同的工业增长率。 萧条时期，英国国民资本净形成与国民生产净值的比率从11.5%下降到6.0%，而德国则从10.6%上升到15.9%。英国采取的是静态供给调整路线，而德国则通过增加和调整资本形成来刺激有效需求，扩大工业供给能力。 例如，德国大幅增加了社会间接资本投资，例如输电线路、公路和铁路的管理，从而刺激了该国的工业需求，但英国的类似投资却停滞或减少。 由此产生的资本形成差异导致了两国工业生产水平的不同以及萧条期间和之后增长率的不同。 [24]

美国和几个欧洲殖民地发现了大量白银，引发了 1873 年的恐慌，白银相对于黄金的价值下降，导致印度本位货币贬值。

在开普殖民地，恐慌导致破产、失业率上升、公共工程暂停以及贸易大幅下滑，一直持续到 1886 年发现黄金。 [25]

在奥斯曼帝国，对外贸易增长率下降，外部贸易条件恶化，小麦价格下跌影响了农民生产者，欧洲对奥斯曼财政的控制导致了巨额海外债务支付。 长期萧条期间农业和总产量的增长率也低于后期。 [26]

拉丁货币联盟

[edit]

白银的普遍非货币化和贬值导致拉丁货币联盟于1873年暂停将白银兑换成硬币。 [27][28]

美国内战（1861-1865）之后出现了铁路建设的繁荣。 1868 年至 1873 年间，全国铺设了 33,000 英里（53,000 公里）的铁轨，[29] 铁路投资热潮很大程度上是由政府土地赠款和铁路补贴推动的。[30]铁路行业是农业以外最大的雇主，涉及大量资金和风险。 投机者的大量资金注入导致了该行业以及码头、工厂和附属设施建设的惊人增长。 大多数资本都参与了不提供立即或早期回报的项目。 [31]

1873 年铸币法

[edit]

北部铁路繁荣引发了一段经济过度扩张时期，随后出现了一系列经济挫折：1869 年的黑色星期五恐慌、1871 年的芝加哥火灾、马流感的爆发和 1872 年的波士顿火灾。

1871 年德意志帝国决定停止铸造塞勒银币，导致需求下降和白银价值下行压力，这反过来又影响了美国，因为大部分白银供应都是在美国开采的。 结果，美国国会通过了1873年的《铸币法案》，改变了国家白银政策。 在该法案出台之前，美国用黄金和白银来支持其货币，并铸造了这两种类型的硬币。 该法案使美国转向事实上的金本位，这意味着美国将不再以法定价格购买白银或将公众的白银转换成银币，但仍会铸造银元以贸易美元的形式出口。 [32]

该法案的直接影响是压低了白银价格，损害了西方采矿业的利益，他们将该法案称为“73年的罪行”，但其影响在一定程度上被亚洲使用的白银贸易美元的引入以及内华达州弗吉尼亚市发现的银矿床所抵消，这导致了对采矿活动的新投资。 [33]该法案还减少了国内货币供应量，提高了利率，损害了农民和其他通常背负沉重债务负担的人。 由此引发的强烈抗议引发了人们对新政策将持续多久的严重质疑。 [34]对美国货币政策不稳定的看法导致投资者回避长期债务，尤其是长期债券。 当时正处于后期阶段的铁路繁荣使问题变得更加复杂。

杰·库克公司失败

[edit]

1873 年 9 月，该国银行机构的主要组成部分杰伊·库克公司 (Jay Cooke & Company) 发现自己无法出售数百万美元的北太平洋铁路债券。 与许多其他公司一样，杰伊·库克的公司对铁路进行了大量投资。 当时一些投资银行急于为其企业提供更多资本。 美国总统尤利西斯·S. 格兰特收缩货币供应从而提高利率的货币政策使债务人的情况变得更糟。 企业在扩张，但为增长提供资金所需的资金却变得越来越稀缺。

库克和其他企业家计划修建第二条横贯大陆的铁路——北太平洋铁路。 库克的公司提供了融资，并于 1870 年 2 月 15 日在明尼苏达州德卢斯附近破土动工。 该铁路公司已从 Jay Cooke & Company 借了超过 150 万美元，但无力偿还。[35]由于信贷银行丑闻，不断扩大的资金缺口变得更难解决。[36]由于欧洲金融危机，库克无法在国外出售证券。 [35] 1873 年 9 月，正当库克即将获得 3 亿美元的政府贷款时，有报道称他的公司的信用几乎变得一文不值。 9月18日，该公司宣布破产。[35][37]

由于财务状况恶化给人寿保险公司带来偿付能力问题，许多美国保险公司倒闭。 幸存公司的共同点是所有的联合养老保险均已上市。[38]

库克银行的倒闭以及不久之后亨利·克鲁斯银行的倒闭引发了银行倒闭的连锁反应，纽约证券交易所暂时关闭。 随着国家陷入萧条，工厂开始裁员。 纽约（25％的工人失业）很快就感受到了恐慌的影响，而芝加哥、弗吉尼亚市、内华达州（银矿开采活跃）和旧金山的影响则较慢。[36][39][40]

纽约证券交易所自 9 月 20 日起休市十天。[41]到 11 月，全国 55 条铁路出现故障，另有 60 条铁路在危机一周年之际破产。 [42]铁路线曾经是经济的支柱之一，但其轨道长度从 1872 年的 7,500 英里（12,100 公里）锐减至 1875 年的仅 1,600 英里（2,600 公里），[42] 1873 年至 1875 年间有 18,000 家企业倒闭。 失业率在 1878 年达到顶峰，达到 8.25%。[43]建筑施工被叫停，工资被削减，房地产价值下降，企业利润消失。 [44]

1874年，国会通过了“渡轮法案”[45]，允许印制货币，增加通货膨胀并降低债务价值。[46]该法案被格兰特总统否决。[46]次年，国会通过了 1875 年《硬币恢复法案》，该法案将以黄金支持美元。 [46]用黄金支持美元有助于抑制通货膨胀并稳定美元。[46]

1873 年之前的几十年里，铁路行业实现了大幅增长，部分原因是欧洲对铁路公司发行的债券产生了浓厚的兴趣。[47][48]大量投资铁路债券的杰伊·库克公司的失败引发了铁路行业的危机。

1877年，工资大幅削减导致铁路工人发起一系列抗议和骚乱，后来被称为“铁路大罢工”。 巴尔的摩和俄亥俄铁路 (B&O) 一年内第三次削减工人工资后，西弗吉尼亚州马丁斯堡爆发了最初的抗议活动。 西弗吉尼亚州州长亨利·M. 马修斯派出了查尔斯·J·马修斯上校率领的民兵。 福克纳试图恢复秩序但没有成功，很大程度上是因为民兵同情工人。 马修斯拜访了卢瑟福·B. 海耶斯请求联邦援助，海耶斯派遣了联邦军队。 这使马丁斯堡恢复了和平，但事实证明存在争议，许多报纸[具体说明]批评马修斯将罢工描述为“叛乱”，而不是绝望和沮丧的行为。 《马丁斯堡政治家》记录了一名罢工工人的观点，他“与其挨饿死，不如死于子弹”。 [49]

一周之内，其他城市也爆发了类似的抗议活动。[50][51]在巴尔的摩，罢工者放火烧毁了 B&O 拥有的建筑物，而数量不足的民兵警卫队在被骚乱者包围时开枪，造成 10 人死亡、25 人受伤，[52] 导致卡姆登庭院发生长达数天的对峙。 在纽约，罢工工人开始向抵达的火车投掷物品，促使当地警方做出反应。 [53]宾夕法尼亚州可能经历了最严重的铁路罢工暴力；[54][55]尤其是 1877 年的匹兹堡铁路罢工、雷丁铁路大屠杀和斯克兰顿总罢工。 在芝加哥，罢工工人导致货运和客运列车停顿，法官托马斯·德拉蒙德下令称此类行为是非法的。 [56]美国法警署的回应是逮捕了数十名罢工者。 在密苏里州，罢工者还导致铁路交通瘫痪，至少有 18 人在冲突中死亡。 [57]

1877 年 7 月，木材市场崩溃，导致几家密歇根木材公司破产。 [58]一年之内，第二次商业衰退的影响一直波及加利福尼亚州。[59]

大萧条于 1879 年春天结束，但工人与银行业和制造业利益领袖之间的紧张关系依然存在。 [60]糟糕的经济状况导致选民转而反对共和党。 在1874年的国会选举中，民主党自内战以来首次控制了众议院。 [61]

舆论使得格兰特政府很难对南方各州制定一致的政策，北方也开始远离重建。 雄心勃勃的铁路建设计划在整个南方都失败了，导致大多数州负债累累，并背负着沉重的税收负担。 紧缩开支是大萧条时期南方对国家债务的常见反应。 南方各州一一落入民主党手中，共和党也失去了权力。

危机的结束恰逢美国移民大潮的开始，这一浪潮一直持续到 1920 年代初期。[62][63]

全球保护主义

[edit]

1873 年经济大萧条后，农业和工业团体游说保护性关税。 俾斯麦等保守派政治家在 1870 年代放弃了古典自由主义经济政策，采取了许多经济干预主义政策，包括高关税、铁路国有化和强制性社会保险。 [64][65][66]政治和经济民族主义也减少了德国和加拿大古典自由党的命运。 法国和英国一样，陷入了长期的停滞，一直持续到 1897 年。 法国人试图通过实施关税来解决经济问题。 法国于 1880 年和 1892 年实施的法律对许多农业和工业进口品征收高额关税。 [67]美国继续奉行保护主义。[68][69]
